stories.headline: A Christian Seaside Resort
stories.hook: Rehoboth Beach began on Jan. 27, 1873, as a Methodist camp meeting by the sea. Within a few years the railroad had changed what kind of place it would be.
stories.lede: Before Rehoboth Beach was a resort town, it was a camp meeting.
stories.body:
Before Rehoboth Beach was a resort town, it was a camp meeting. Its founders did not set out to build a beach destination. They set out to build a place for summer religious gatherings that happened to be beside the ocean.

A charter from the Legislature

On Jan. 27, 1873, the Delaware Legislature incorporated the Rehoboth Beach Camp Meeting Association of the Methodist Episcopal Church. The effort was led by the Rev. Robert W. Todd, and its stated purpose was to maintain a permanent camp-meeting ground and a "Christian sea-side resort."

The association bought more than 400 acres from local farmers. In its first year it laid out its encampment grounds, with small wooden structures known as "tents," and the original Rehoboth boardwalk was built in 1873.

The railroad changes everything

The camp meeting's undoing was its own success at drawing people to the shore. When the railroad reached Rehoboth in 1878, development accelerated and visitors arrived in far greater numbers, most of them more interested in the beach than in religious meetings. The association's camp meetings ended in 1881.

From Cape Henlopen City to Rehoboth Beach

The town that grew up in the camp meeting's place took a few tries to settle on a name. In 1891 the General Assembly incorporated it as Cape Henlopen City. After controversy and reorganization, it was renamed Rehoboth Beach in 1893.

What remains

Very little of the camp meeting era still stands, and the boardwalk is not the one built in 1873. But the shape of the founding is still in the town's story. In January 2023, Rehoboth marked 150 years since the camp meeting association was founded, with a commemoration of the town's religious beginnings.

Rehoboth today is a long way from a Methodist retreat. It is worth remembering, on an off-season walk along the boardwalk, that the first one was built for people who had come to the shore for a different reason.

Sources: The Delaware Public Archives' City of Rehoboth Beach historical marker; Cape Gazette coverage of the 150th anniversary of the camp meeting association's founding (2023), including the Jan. 27, 1873 incorporation and the 1881 end of the camp meetings; the Rehoboth Beach-Dewey Beach Chamber of Commerce's area history for the 1873 encampment, tents and boardwalk and the 1878 railroad; town histories for the 1891 Cape Henlopen City incorporation and the 1893 renaming. Delaware Beach Finds did not attend the anniversary events.

stories.headline: Rebuilding a Marsh at Prime Hook
stories.hook: After Hurricane Sandy broke through the dunes at Prime Hook National Wildlife Refuge, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service rebuilt about 4,000 acres of tidal marsh.
stories.lede: On the Delaware Bay shore north of Lewes, a wildlife refuge was rebuilt from the sand up.
stories.body:
On the Delaware Bay shore north of Lewes, a wildlife refuge was rebuilt from the sand up.

A refuge for migratory birds

Prime Hook National Wildlife Refuge was established in Sussex County in 1963 under the Migratory Bird Conservation Act, as a sanctuary for migratory birds. It began as a satellite of Bombay Hook National Wildlife Refuge, its sister refuge farther up the bay. It is managed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

What the storms did

Prime Hook sits behind a long stretch of barrier beach along the Delaware Bay. Storms broke through that beach and cut deep channels into the marsh behind it. Hurricane Sandy, in 2012, did the worst of the damage.

The restoration

The Fish and Wildlife Service's answer was a $38 million marsh restoration, completed in 2016. It was designed not just to repair the damage from Sandy but to build resilience to storms and sea-level rise into the landscape itself.

The work restored about 4,000 acres of back-barrier tidal marsh. Crews carved miles of marsh drainage channels, mostly following historic drainage patterns, and pumped about 1.1 million cubic yards of sand along some 7,000 feet of shoreline to fill the deep cuts the storms had left. The Service describes it as the largest tidal marsh restoration project ever undertaken in the eastern United States.

Why a marsh matters here

A healthy tidal marsh behind a barrier beach supports the beach itself, and it is the habitat the refuge exists to protect. The refuge was created for migrating birds, and on the Delaware Bay shore the marsh is where much of that habitat lies.

Seeing it

Prime Hook is a working refuge, and its trails, roads, hours and seasonal closures are set by the Fish and Wildlife Service. Check the refuge's current information before you go. For a wider look at the bay's refuges and how the marshes are changing, see our earlier stories on the refuge loop and on where the marsh is going.

Sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service: Prime Hook National Wildlife Refuge "About Us" (fws.gov) for the 1963 establishment under the Migratory Bird Conservation Act and its origin as a satellite of Bombay Hook; the Service's "Marsh Restoration at Prime Hook National Wildlife Refuge" project page and its tidal marsh and dune restoration summary for the $38 million project completed in 2016, Hurricane Sandy, the roughly 4,000 acres, the channels, the 1.1 million cubic yards of sand along 7,000 feet of shoreline and the largest-in-the-East description. Delaware Beach Finds did not visit the refuge for this story. Access is the refuge's to set.
